The Icterine warbler (Hippolais icterina) is a small passerine that undertakes long-distance migrations between European breeding grounds and sub-Saharan African wintering areas. Field studies have documented that newly hatched nestlings emerge at a remarkably modest initial wet weight of 1.7 grams [Ww0 = 1.7 grams], a value consistent with the altricial development pattern typical of sylviid warblers. Under controlled incubation conditions maintained at 30 °C [T = 30 °C], the age at birth, defined as the moment of hatching from the calcareous egg, occurs after approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days]. This incubation period places the species within the expected range for its body size among Old World warblers. During this embryonated egg stage, the developing chick relies entirely on yolk reserves, and the thermal environment of the nest plays a critical role in determining the timing of this first major developmental transition from the incubated bird egg to the altricial nestling.

Once hatched, the nestling chick enters a phase of rapid somatic growth that is heavily dependent on the provisioning efforts of both parents. The ultimate wet weight for females in this species reaches an average of 13.2 grams [Wwi = 13.2 grams], with a documented range of 11 to 16 grams across different populations and breeding seasons. This asymptotic adult body mass is relatively modest compared to other members of the Acrocephalidae family and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by an insectivorous diet. The progression from a hatchling mass of 1.7 grams [Ww0 = 1.7 grams] to the adult female mass of 13.2 grams [Wwi = 13.2 grams] represents an approximately 7.8-fold increase, a growth multiple that is characteristic of small passerines with a brief nestling period. This accelerated growth phase requires sustained high feeding rates from the provisioning adult, particularly during the feather-growing nestling stage.

Under the thermal conditions associated with active metabolic periods in this species, specifically at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable series of developmental milestones unfolds during the early post-hatching period. Fledging, marked by the achievement of first flight and nest departure, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling period that allows the developing chick to escape the high predation pressure typical of open-cup nests in shrubland habitats at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Following nest departure, the fledgling enters a period of post-fledging dispersal and continued feather maturation, during which it remains dependent on parental provisioning for several weeks before achieving nutritional independence. This accelerated fledging schedule is advantageous for a migratory species that must complete its pre-migratory fattening before autumn departure.

Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], sexual maturation in the Icterine warbler proceeds gradually after the fledgling independence stage. Field observations indicate that the time since birth at puberty, defined by the initiation of gonadal activity and the onset of gametogenesis, is reached at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively early attainment of reproductive maturity, occurring well within the first year of life, allows young birds to potentially breed in the spring following their hatching year. However, the time since birth at first brood, representing the age at which a female successfully produces her first clutch, is deferred to 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This one-year delay between the onset of puberty and actual first reproduction reflects the constraints of territory acquisition, mate selection, and the energetic demands of migration on a young bird's ability to successfully rear offspring.

The reproductive output of the Icterine warbler reflects its life-history strategy as a small, short-lived passerine. Females typically lay a clutch of 4 to 5 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 4 to 5 eggs], and under favorable conditions, they may produce one brood per breeding season [F_R_i = one brood per breeding season]. The maximum recorded longevity in the wild, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], is approximately 3,942 days [am = approximately 3,942 days], a value that corresponds to nearly 10.8 years of life. This extended lifespan potential is notable for a small warbler and may be linked to the species' relatively low annual adult mortality during migration, as well as its ability to exploit diverse habitats across its range. Basal oxygen consumption measurements at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] indicate a maximum resting metabolic rate of 84.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 84.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the allometric expectations for a passerine of its size. Such a metabolic rate underscores the high energetic demands of a small-bodied insectivore engaged in long-distance migration and biparental care of altricial young.
